# Portfolio Case Study: Leakage-Aware Prioritisation of Content Pages for Editorial Review

**Umer Sajid · Junior ML · Prototype Study**

---

## What This Project Is

This case study documents a random-forest prototype I built to rank anonymised content pages by their likelihood of warranting editorial review. The core methodological challenge was **data leakage**: in content datasets, pages belonging to the same client share structural and stylistic patterns, so a naïve train/test split inflates apparent performance. I addressed this by holding out **seven pseudonymised clients in their entirety**, ensuring the model was evaluated only on client relationships it had never seen during training.

The public-safe dataset contains approximately **30,000 pages across 32 pseudonymised clients**.

---

## What the Evaluation Shows

On the held-out client split, the model achieved a **Precision@50 of 0.540**, compared to **0.340 for a transparent baseline** — meaning that of the 50 pages the model ranked highest for review, 54% were confirmed candidates, versus 34% under the baseline. That gap is the evidence this study rests on.

---

## What This Result Does and Does Not Claim

The Precision@50 improvement supports using the model to generate a **review-for-refresh queue** that an editorial team acts on. It does not demonstrate traffic recovery, establish causation between page edits and any downstream metric, or justify autonomous page changes. A human editor remains the decision-maker.

---

*The sections that follow cover feature engineering, the leakage control design, and honest limitations.*

# Leakage-Aware Evaluation of a Content-Page Prioritisation Prototype

## Case Study Introduction

Editorial teams that refresh ageing content face a triage problem: which pages deserve attention first? Ranking models can help, but only if their evaluation is honest about what the numbers actually show.

I built a random-forest prototype designed to score anonymised content pages by their candidacy for editorial review. The public-safe starter dataset covers roughly 30,000 pages spread across 32 pseudonymised clients. To prevent leakage from inflating the results, I held out seven pseudonymised clients entirely — those clients contributed no signal to training, so the validation split reflects how the model would behave on an organisation it has never encountered.

On that held-out split, the model reached a Precision@50 of 0.540, compared with 0.340 for a transparent baseline evaluated under the same conditions. The gap is meaningful enough to support using the ranked output as a review-for-refresh queue, where an editor decides what action, if any, each flagged page warrants.

What the comparison cannot show: it does not demonstrate that refreshing flagged pages recovers traffic, establishes causation between any page characteristic and performance, or justifies autonomous changes. The prototype is an editorial prioritisation aid, and the evaluation was scoped accordingly.

The sections that follow document the feature design, the leakage controls, and the limits I placed on interpreting the output.

Leakage-Aware Evaluation of a Random-Forest Prototype for Prioritising Content Pages Across Held-Out Clients: Precision@50 0.540 vs. Baseline 0.340

---

**(2) Introduction**

I built a random-forest prototype to rank anonymised content pages by their suitability for editorial review. To avoid data leakage, I held out seven pseudonymised clients entirely during training, so the validation set contained organisations the model had never encountered. The public-safe dataset covers roughly 30,000 pages across 32 pseudonymised clients.

On that held-out split, the model reached a Precision@50 of 0.540, meaning 27 of the top 50 ranked pages were flagged as review-worthy. ---

**(3) Limitation**

This comparison shows that the model prioritises pages more accurately than the baseline on held-out clients; it does not show that acting on the queue will recover traffic or cause any measurable content outcome.
